question: How could the U.S. leave each international organization?
answer: Each of the 27 bodies has its own exit route. Where the founding text names a period, it runs from immediately (Board of Peace) and on receipt of notice (International Monetary Fund) to 90 days (Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons), six months (World Trade Organization, World Intellectual Property Organization), one year (NATO, OECD, International Civil Aviation Organization, International Maritime Organization, International Telecommunication Union) and two years (Organization of American States). For NATO the record adds: 'U.S. domestic statute requires Senate or Congress route'. 3 name a notice route without a period in the record (International Atomic Energy Agency, World Bank Group, ITER). 6 have no simple withdrawal clause (the United Nations Charter has none) and 4 are not memberships the U.S. could leave. 3 exits already carry a date: World Health Organization, UNESCO, Paris Agreement; the WHO exit, stated effective January 22, 2026, is disputed.

Percentages are institution-specific and cannot be consolidated. Exit, defunding, internal refit, parallel doctrine, shared machinery, resource migration, default use and residual-incumbent status are separate clocks.
The notice-period groups are read from each body's exit wording in the registry; the wording itself is printed on every card and in the table.
Notice is not effectiveness, and defunding is not exit: the U.S. exit clock column comes from the map's exit clocks, not from the clause.
The registry holds no web links; the instruments behind each exit clause are named in the package's wave ledgers.

catalog_context.title: How the United States participates in and can leave international organizations
catalog_context.answer: The international order is changing one job at a time. Countries are leaving some bodies, rebuilding others and creating smaller groups for specific tasks; they are not replacing the whole system at once.
